taxonomy: UK Finance Annual Fraud Report - eight APP scam types
headline_figures: Annual Fraud Report 2026 (2025 data), as printed: Total APP £576.4m (+19%), 248,070 cases (+7%); all fraud £1.28bn (+4%), 4.06M confirmed cases (+11%). By type, Value / Cases (YoY change): Purchase £118.1m (20%) / 175,809 (5%); Investment £221.5m (40%) / 14,893 (26%); Romance £39.2m (23%) / 6,335 (22%); Advance fee £58.4m (65%) / 24,080 (38%); Invoice & mandate £41.3m (-4%) / 2,305 (-2%); CEO £5.6m (-53%) / 197 (-29%); Impersonation police/bank staff £55.5m (-18%) / 6,016 (-23%); Impersonation other £36.9m (-1%) / 18,435 (-7%). 71% of APP cases were purchase scams; 38% of APP losses were investment scams. 66% of fraud cases enabled online (32% of losses); 17% enabled by telecommunications (28% of losses). Reimbursement 2025: purchase 78%, investment 48%, romance 67%, advance fee 60%, invoice & mandate 48%, CEO 20%, impersonation police/bank 80%, impersonation other 80%.
notes: Per-type figures taken from each section header (pages 38-45 of the PDF); the annex table text extraction is column-misaligned, so do not use it. As printed: the four malicious-payee types (victim knowingly pays the scammer) each hit record losses in 2025 and combined rose 35% to £437 million; malicious-redirection types now account for 'just under a quarter' of APP losses (down from over half in 2020). UK Finance notes investment-scam victims tend to proceed regardless of payment warnings and that these scams start with small payments that grow - the gap a Ruko voice call targets. Police/bank impersonation hit its lowest-ever loss and case totals in 2025, attributed to Take Five messaging and in-journey warnings. Since PSR mandatory reimbursement (Oct 2024) UK Finance no longer publishes CRM-code data. Courier scams are counted under card fraud (UK retail face-to-face), not APP.

taxonomy: Action Fraud (now Report Fraud) fraud types + PSR APP reimbursement rules (Oct 2024)
types: financial investment fraud / share sales and boiler room fraud
mandate fraud / payment diversion fraud / business email compromise
headline_figures: PSR rules as printed on its consumer page: payments on or after 7 October 2024 via Faster Payments or CHAPS; individuals, microenterprises and charities; maximum reimbursement £85,000 (stated to cover over 99% of claims); optional excess up to £100 (not for vulnerable consumers); claim within 13 months; reimburse within 5 business days, up to 35 business days with stop-the-clock; exceptions for complicity, gross negligence (not applied to vulnerable consumers) and civil disputes. PSR 'One year on' (08/10/2025): 88% of money lost and claimed back returned; £112 million returned in first nine months; 126,000 claims Oct 2024-Jun 2025; 84% resolved within five business days.
notes: Action Fraud was replaced by Report Fraud (City of London Police) on 4 December 2025 (GOV.UK); actionfraud.police.uk URLs redirect to reportfraud.police.uk and block WebFetch (403), the A-Z was read in a browser. The A-Z is a police reporting taxonomy (it mixes consumer scams with business/insider/tax fraud); only the consumer-scam types are listed here. PSR reimbursement covers only UK-to-UK Faster Payments/CHAPS, so international wires, card, cash and crypto (courier fraud cash, Bitcoin ATMs, gift cards) fall outside it - a reason a pre-payment hold like Ruko matters most on those rails. The UK Finance 2026 report confirms the rules took effect October 2024 and that its own data covers wider payment types than the PSR scope.

Mortgage Foreclosure Relief and Debt Management
Foreign Money Offers and Fake Check Scams
payment methods: Credit Cards, Payment App or Service, Debit Card, Bank Transfer or Payment, Cryptocurrency, Gift Card or Reload Card, Wire Transfer, Cash, Check, Money Order
headline_figures: Data Book 2024 (March 2025; latest full edition found): 6.47 million total reports; 2.6 million fraud reports, 38% with a loss; over $12 billion lost (stated as more than $12.5 billion in the FTC March 2025 press release); top 3 report categories Credit Bureaus (20.91%), Identity Theft (17.54%), Imposter Scams (845,806 reports, 13.07%, $2.95 billion lost). Median fraud loss $497; Investment Related median $9,196. Payment method, reports / total loss: Credit Cards 108,881 / $275M; Payment App or Service 90,571 / $391M; Debit Card 76,285 / $180M; Bank Transfer or Payment 47,336 / $2,089M; Cryptocurrency 46,899 / $1,417M; Gift Card or Reload Card 41,120 / $212M; Wire Transfer 40,448 / $287M; Cash 13,609 / $308M; Check 8,098 / $225M; Money Order 2,658 / $51M. Full-year 2025 (FTC JEC testimony, 25 March 2026): 3 million fraud reports, $15.9 billion lost; imposter scams over 1 million reports and over $3.5 billion; investment scams over $7.9 billion (about half of losses); bank payments highest aggregate losses, then cryptocurrency; text the top contact method; social media top by losses (over $2 billion, FY 2025). FTC June 15, 2026 release: government impersonators about $920 million, business impersonators nearly $1 billion in 2025.
notes: A 'Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2025' PDF/page was not found on ftc.gov (expected URLs returned 404 and the Sentinel reports index still lists 2024 as latest), so 2025 figures come from the FTC's March 2026 testimony and 2026 press releases; FTC also publishes live data on Tableau Public. Sentinel categories are reporting buckets, not mechanisms (e.g. family/grandparent and tech-support scams sit inside Imposter Scams). The payment rails Ruko can hold (bank transfer, wire) carry the largest US dollar losses; crypto, gift cards and cash are the rails victims are pushed toward, often via a bank withdrawal Ruko can see first.

types: contact channels: text/SMS, phone, email, social media, website, in-person
headline_figures: Targeting Scams Report 2025 (NASC, released 30 Mar 2026; calendar 2025, combined Scamwatch/ReportCyber/AFCX/IDCARE/ASIC data): 481,523 reports; 274,577 with losses totalling $2.18 billion (AUD); losses +7.8% vs 2024 and -29.7% from the $3.1 billion 2022 peak. Top five by loss: investment $837.7m, payment re-direction $166.8m, romance $139.9m, phishing $97.6m, remote access $69.9m (together 60% of losses). Most-reported Scamwatch scam: phishing (65,361 reports). Ages 65+ accounted for 26.5% of Scamwatch losses. Text-message scam reports fell from 77,365 (2024) to 29,058 (2025). Scamwatch types page: phone scams cost Australians $141 million 'last year' (year not stated on page).
notes: Scamwatch and nasc.gov.au/accc.gov.au block WebFetch (403); pages were read in a browser, the full report PDF was not opened. The NASC top-5-by-loss list uses finer categories than the 13 public 'types' (e.g. payment re-direction and remote access are named in the report but fall under BEC and threat/takeover on the types page). 'Hi Mum' family impersonation and government/bank impersonation appear under text/SMS and phone channel guidance rather than as a separate type.

types: business email compromise scams (SPF key concern)
headline_figures: SPF Mid-Year Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2026 (26 Aug 2026), 1H 2026 vs 1H 2025, cases / losses: E-commerce 3,865 / S$8.3M (3,240 / S$7.0M); Phishing 3,104 / S$9.6M (3,772 / S$30.0M); Investment 2,256 / S$169.8M (2,692 / S$178.9M); Job 2,247 / S$34.9M (2,717 / S$64.0M); Government officials impersonation 1,363 / S$90.8M (1,772 / S$132.9M); Social media impersonation 587 / S$3.9M (397 / S$2.2M); Sexual services 478 / S$1.5M; Loan 384 / S$2.1M; Internet love 373 / S$8.4M (428 / S$12.2M); Fake friend call 353 / S$818K (1,052 / S$3.0M). BEC 262 cases / S$57.3M (+193.1% losses). Total scams 16,821 cases (-14.4%), about S$410.6 million (-17.9%); 80.8% self-effected transfers; median loss S$1,350; elderly average loss $42,347. Full-year 2025 (SPF, 25 Feb 2026): scam and cybercrime cases 41,974 (-24.8%), losses S$913.1 million; 81.8% self-effected transfers. ScamShield: crypto-related scams S$182.2M in 2025 (20% of losses).
notes: ScamShield's home page states 16,281 1H-2026 scam cases while the SPF PDF states 16,821 - use the PDF figure. Self-effected transfers above 80% means most Singapore scam losses are victim-initiated payments of the kind a Ruko hold-and-call can intercept. GOIS victims are mostly 65+ (40.8%) and are increasingly told to make ATM cash deposits or hand over cash, gold and luxury watches to mules; banks in SG now push in-app notifications to verify genuine bank calls and the government is piloting a single recognisable call prefix.
